info.summary: Search backend for Findling: text extraction, OCR and the index
Suchdienst für Findling: Textauszug, Texterkennung und der Index
Service de recherche pour Findling : extraction de texte, OCR et index
info.description:
This is the External App behind the Findling search app.
It extracts text from documents, runs OCR on scanned pages and maintains the search index. All of that happens inside your own instance: no file content ever leaves the server, and nothing is ever written back to your files.
This app does nothing on its own. It needs the app "AppAPI", which installs and runs it, and the app "Findling", which puts the results into the normal search bar and is the only caller of this backend. Once both are there, nothing has to be configured: the first index starts by itself, and scanned documents are read with OCR without a setting being touched.
What it costs in memory, measured: A full index and OCR run over 50,000 files and 20 GB on a 4-GB box peaked at 429 MB of resident anonymous memory, under a hard 2 GB limit enforced by the kernel, with no OOM kill. The machine was x86 and the repetition on ARM hardware is still open; the report docs/performance.md in the source code carries the method, the curve and every figure that repetition will replace.
Privacy: everything runs locally in this container on your own machine. No file content ever leaves the server, and there is no telemetry of any kind, not even a version check. What is stored, so that nobody has to guess: the text extracted from every indexed document is kept in this app's own volume, because the short excerpts shown under a search result are cut out of it on demand. A backup of that volume, including the ones an all-in-one setup takes, therefore contains the text of your indexed documents, and the index is not encrypted at rest, which is a matter for the host it runs on.

Dies ist die External App hinter der Such-App Findling.
Sie gewinnt Text aus Dokumenten, liest gescannte Seiten per Texterkennung und pflegt den Suchindex. All das geschieht innerhalb Ihrer eigenen Instanz: kein Dateiinhalt verlässt den Server, und in Ihre Dateien wird nie etwas zurückgeschrieben.
Diese App tut von sich aus nichts. Sie braucht die App "AppAPI", die sie installiert und betreibt, und die App "Findling", die die Ergebnisse in die gewöhnliche Suchleiste bringt und der einzige Aufrufer dieses Dienstes ist. Sind beide vorhanden, muss nichts eingerichtet werden: Der erste Indexlauf beginnt von selbst, und gescannte Dokumente werden per Texterkennung gelesen, ohne dass eine Einstellung angefasst wird.
Was es an Arbeitsspeicher kostet, gemessen: Ein vollständiger Index- und Texterkennungslauf über 50.000 Dateien und 20 GB auf einer 4-GB-Box hatte seine Spitze bei 429 MB anonymem Arbeitsspeicher, unter einer harten Grenze von 2 GB, die der Kernel durchsetzt, und ohne einen einzigen Abschuss wegen Speichermangels. Die Maschine war x86, die Wiederholung auf ARM-Hardware steht aus; der Bericht docs/performance.md im Quellcode nennt die Methode, die Kurve und jede Zahl, die diese Wiederholung ersetzen wird.
Datenschutz: Alles läuft lokal in diesem Container auf Ihrer eigenen Maschine. Kein Dateiinhalt verlässt den Server, und es gibt keinerlei Telemetrie, nicht einmal eine Versionsabfrage. Was gespeichert wird, damit niemand raten muss: Der aus jedem indexierten Dokument gewonnene Text liegt im eigenen Datenspeicher dieser App, weil die kurzen Auszüge unter einem Suchtreffer bei Bedarf daraus geschnitten werden. Eine Sicherung dieses Datenspeichers, auch die einer All-in-One-Installation, enthält damit den Text Ihrer indexierten Dokumente, und der Index ist im Ruhezustand nicht verschlüsselt, was Sache des Wirtssystems ist.

Ceci est l'External App qui se trouve derrière l'application de recherche Findling.
Elle extrait le texte des documents, lit les pages numérisées par reconnaissance optique de caractères et tient à jour l'index de recherche. Tout cela se passe à l'intérieur de votre propre instance : aucun contenu de fichier ne quitte le serveur, et rien n'est jamais réécrit dans vos fichiers.
Cette application ne fait rien d'elle-même. Elle a besoin de l'application "AppAPI", qui l'installe et la fait tourner, et de l'application "Findling", qui place les résultats dans la barre de recherche habituelle et qui est le seul appelant de ce service. Une fois les deux en place, il n'y a rien à configurer : la première indexation démarre d'elle-même, et les documents numérisés sont lus par reconnaissance optique sans qu'un seul réglage soit touché.
Ce que cela coûte en mémoire, mesuré : une indexation complète avec reconnaissance optique portant sur 50 000 fichiers et 20 Go sur une machine de 4 Go a culminé à 429 Mo de mémoire anonyme résidente, sous une limite stricte de 2 Go imposée par le noyau, et sans la moindre interruption pour manque de mémoire. La machine était en x86, la répétition sur du matériel ARM reste à faire ; le rapport docs/performance.md dans le code source donne la méthode, la courbe et chaque chiffre que cette répétition remplacera.
Confidentialité : tout fonctionne localement dans ce conteneur, sur votre propre machine. Aucun contenu de fichier ne quitte le serveur, et il n'y a aucune télémétrie, pas même une vérification de version. Ce qui est conservé, pour que personne n'ait à le deviner : le texte extrait de chaque document indexé est gardé dans le volume propre de cette application, parce que les courts extraits affichés sous un résultat de recherche y sont découpés à la demande. Une sauvegarde de ce volume, y compris celle que prend une installation tout-en-un, contient donc le texte de vos documents indexés, et l'index n'est pas chiffré au repos, ce qui relève de l'hôte sur lequel il tourne.

variable.name: FINDLING_LOG_LEVEL
variable.description: One of debug, info, warning, error. Anything else falls back to info.

variable.name: FINDLING_LANGUAGES
variable.description: Comma separated, currently de and en. Changing this changes how text is broken into words, so the index has to be built again afterwards: until it is, older documents answer differently from newer ones, which looks like "my hits are gone". An empty or unknown value keeps de,en.

variable.name: FINDLING_COMPOUND_DICT
variable.description: full or nouns. Measured: full has 276496 entries and finds 14 of 16 test compounds through one of their parts; nouns has 86345 entries, finds 12 of 16 and needs roughly two thirds less memory for the splitting automaton, which is worth having on a small box. Like the language list, this changes how text is broken into words and requires the index to be built again.

variable.name: FINDLING_MAX_FILE_BYTES
variable.description: In bytes, 52428800 is 50 MB. Larger files are skipped while the file list is walked, so they never cost the container anything. Raising this raises the peak memory of one extraction. Anything that is not a positive whole number falls back to the default.

variable.name: FINDLING_OCR_ENABLED
variable.description: true or false. When this is off, scanned PDFs and images are still listed by name but their content is not read, and everything else about the indexing stays exactly as it is. Turn it off on a very slow machine where the indexing queue never catches up. Anything that is not a yes or no value keeps OCR on.

variable.name: FINDLING_OCR_LANGUAGES
variable.description: Joined with a plus sign, in the order of importance, for example deu+eng or deu. Only the languages this image carries are accepted, which today are deu (German) and eng (English); anything else is ignored with a warning in the log and never reaches the engine. Note that this is not the same setting as the index languages above: this one decides how a scan is read, that one decides how any text is broken into words.

variable.name: FINDLING_OCR_MAX_PAGES
variable.description: A whole number between 1 and 500. Beyond it the document is indexed with the pages read so far and marked as shortened, rather than skipped: a 200 page scan stays findable through its first 30 pages. The default of 30 keeps one batch of the indexing queue below its lock timeout, so raising it a lot without also raising that timeout makes large scans look stuck. Anything outside the range falls back to the default.

variable.name: FINDLING_OCR_PAGE_SECONDS
variable.description: A whole number between 1 and 300. A page that takes longer is dropped and the next one is read. Measured on a laptop core, a clean A4 page at 300 dpi takes about two seconds; the default of 30 is meant to cut off the outlier on a slow ARM board, not the normal page.

variable.name: FINDLING_OCR_JOB_SECONDS
variable.description: A whole number between 1 and 780. When the budget is spent the document is indexed with what was read so far and marked as shortened. The hard limit at which the whole job is abandoned is always this value plus 60 seconds, so that the partial text has a window to be handed over; that is why it is not a setting of its own. The ceiling of 780 keeps a claimed batch of two OCR jobs safely under the 1800 second queue lock; anything outside the range falls back to the default.

variable.name: FINDLING_OCR_DPI
variable.display-name: Resolution used to read a scanned page
variable.description: A whole number between 72 and 600. 300 is what the engine works best with. Lower values are faster and read worse; higher ones cost memory with the square of the number, which is why the ceiling exists at all. Anything outside the range falls back to the default.

variable.name: FINDLING_RECONCILE_ENABLED
variable.display-name: Check the index against the file list
variable.description: true or false. When this is on, Findling walks the file list once a day and repairs whatever the live updates missed: files that were added or changed without an event reaching the app, and files that were removed while it was not running. Turning it off means the index is only ever as good as the stream of events, and a lost event then stays lost until the next full re-index. Anything that is not a yes or no value keeps the check on.

variable.name: FINDLING_RECONCILE_HOUR
variable.description: A whole number between 0 and 23, in the time zone of the container. The check waits for this hour before it starts a full walk. If the container is switched off at that hour, the walk starts anyway once twice the pause below has gone by, so that the guarantee is not lost on a machine that only runs during the day. Anything outside the range falls back to 2.

variable.name: FINDLING_RECONCILE_MIN_INTERVAL_HOURS
variable.description: A whole number of hours. At most one full walk over the file list happens in this span. Raising it on a very large instance makes the check cheaper and the repair slower; lowering it below a day rarely pays, because live updates already carry the day to day changes. Anything that is not a positive whole number falls back to 24.

variable.name: FINDLING_RECONCILE_QUIET_MAX
variable.description: A whole number of waiting queue entries. Above it the check stands down and tries again later, so that it never competes with a first indexing run or a backlog of scanned documents. The default of 100 is about three batches of the indexing worker. Raising it makes the check more insistent on a busy instance; lowering it to 1 means it only ever runs on a completely empty queue.

variable.name: FINDLING_RECONCILE_SLICE
variable.display-name: Files per page of the check
variable.description: A whole number between 1 and 2000. The file list is read in pages of this size, with a short breather between them, which is what keeps the check bearable outside the quiet hours. Larger pages are faster and heavier on the Nextcloud database; the server side caps this at 2000 in any case. Anything outside the range falls back to 500.
